title: Does every point set admit an oriented t-spanner with t < 2?
formal: Is there a real constant t<2 such that, for every integer d≥1 and every finite set P⊆ℝ^d with |P|≥3, some oriented graph on P has oriented dilation at most t? Edges may join arbitrary pairs, with Euclidean lengths, but opposite directed edges on the same pair are forbidden.
why: The historical question tested how much detour is forced by one-way connections when every pair needs a short round trip. The 5/3 theorem crosses its proposed threshold and now serves as a benchmark for stronger dilation, sparsity and optimization questions.
status_note: Resolved positively by Bhore et al., Sparse Oriented Spanners in Metric Spaces, ESA 2026, Theorem 6, published 25 August 2026. The theorem gives t=5/3<2 for every finite metric point set, including the Euclidean point sets in the original question. Corollary 10 also answers the linear-size version in fixed-dimensional Euclidean spaces. The original and later definitions and theorem statements were matched on 11 September 2026; this is a published-result assessment, not an independent proof audit.

progress.text: Buchin and coauthors leave the universal t<2 target open, even for complete orientations.

Bhore and coauthors, Theorem 6, prove the universal bound 5/3 for finite metric spaces. Corollary 10 yields sparse 5/3+ε spanners under its metric-decomposition hypothesis, including fixed-dimensional Euclidean point sets.

importance.reason: A specific universal dilation threshold for one-way geometric connections, now settled by a stronger metric-space theorem; its historical value is to distinguish existence guarantees from optimal-orientation complexity. The prior numerical score is preserved.

sentences: An oriented spanner assigns at most one direction to each connection between two points.
Its dilation compares the shortest directed round trip through each pair with the perimeter of that pair’s cheapest triangle.
The historical question asks for one factor strictly below two that works for every point set.
The published ESA 2026 theorem answers positively with factor five thirds, even in general finite metric spaces.
Finding an orientation with the smallest possible dilation for a particular point set remains a separate question.

definitions: An oriented graph on P has no loops and, for each unordered pair {p,q}, includes either no edge or exactly one of p→q and q→p. A directed walk follows the directions of its edges; its length is the sum of their Euclidean lengths, counting repeated traversals. It is closed if it ends where it starts. For distinct p,q∈P, let C_G(p,q) be the minimum length of a directed closed walk containing both p and q, or +∞ if none exists. Define Δ_P(p,q)=min_{r∈P\{p,q}} (‖p−q‖₂+‖q−r‖₂+‖r−p‖₂), the minimum perimeter of a triangle using p, q and a third point of P. Here ‖x‖₂=√(Σ_i x_i²). Since P contains at least three distinct points, this denominator is finite and positive. The oriented dilation is max_{p≠q} C_G(p,q)/Δ_P(p,q). An oriented t-spanner has dilation at most t. The constant t is independent of the point set, its size and dimension. The target imposes no planarity, sparsity or running-time restriction; choosing an orientation of the complete graph is permitted. A tournament means such a complete orientation. The published solution holds more generally with any metric distance, namely a symmetric nonnegative distance that vanishes exactly on equal points and obeys the triangle inequality.
answer_criterion: The historical assertion is answered positively by the published choice t=5/3. Theorem 6 constructs a tournament with this bound for every finite metric point set. A claim about only average dilation, a prescribed sparse input graph, or a point-set-dependent bound approaching two would have had a different conclusion.

context_blocks.text: Imagine assigning one-way connections between locations while keeping every round trip reasonably short. The condition concerns a closed walk through each pair, so it controls travel in both directions together. An edge may not be used in both directions; going from p to q and back generally needs a third location.

The reference length is the cheapest triangle through the pair using another point from the same set. For three points, orienting their triangle cyclically gives dilation one: the only directed round trip has exactly the reference perimeter. A transitive orientation of those three points contains no directed cycle and gives infinite dilation. This illustrates why edge direction matters even when every pair is connected.

The original 2025 question asked whether the universal factor could be made strictly smaller than two, including when all pairs were available for orientation. It did not require an optimal orientation or a plane drawing without crossings.

Bhore and coauthors answer this target with factor 5/3 in Theorem 6 of their ESA 2026 paper. Their theorem applies to every finite metric space and supplies a complete orientation. Their Corollary 10 also gives factor 5/3+ε with a linear number of edges in fixed-dimensional Euclidean spaces; choosing a fixed ε<1/3 keeps this factor below two.

Computing a minimum-dilation tournament is a separate optimization question, retained as TCS-1212. A uniform upper bound supplies a good orientation without determining the best one for each point set. The 2026 paper explicitly leaves that optimization complexity open.
